title: Technical Leadership & Communication
requirement: Strong technical leadership, structured problem-solving, written communication skills.

questions.question: How is a technical lead role different from a senior engineer role?
questions.answer: A senior engineer's success is the systems they build. A lead's is what the whole team ships and how it evolves without them. I still code, but my best work is unblocking others and keeping the architecture coherent. I influence more than I control.
questions.keyTakeaway: Lead success is team output and system coherence, not personal throughput.

questions.question: How do you set technical direction across both front-end and back-end teams?
questions.answer: I start from shared product goals and set a few priorities every team aligns on, like API contracts, observability, and release discipline, instead of dictating stacks. I publish short decisions with their context, set contracts at the seams early, and handle exceptions through design review.
questions.keyTakeaway: Few published decisions with context, hard contracts at the seams, exceptions through review.

questions.question: Describe your structured approach when handed an ambiguous technical problem.
questions.answer: I write the problem statement in one paragraph and get it corrected, because half of ambiguity is people solving different problems. Then I split it into knowns, unknowns, and constraints, and attack the unknowns with cheap experiments, not debate. I lay out at least two options with trade-offs, decide, and record a checkpoint to revisit.
questions.keyTakeaway: Written problem statement, experiments over debate, options with trade-offs, decision with a checkpoint.

questions.question: Why does the posting emphasize written communication, and how do you practice it?
questions.answer: Distributed decisions live or die in writing. An RFC brings vagueness into the open and gives every timezone the same input. Mine are under two pages: problem, options, recommendation, risks. The test is whether a new engineer can act on it without asking me.
questions.keyTakeaway: RFCs make decisions reviewable and permanent; a doc that still needs you is not done.

questions.question: A senior engineer disagrees with your architectural decision openly. What do you do?
questions.answer: I take it seriously and do it in the open, because the team watches how disagreement gets handled. I ask them to argue the alternative with concrete criteria like cost, risk, and operability. If their case is stronger, I change the decision visibly. If mine stands, I explain why. I never win by title.
questions.keyTakeaway: Disagree with criteria in the open, reverse yourself when wrong, never win by title.

questions.question: How do you balance hands-on coding with leadership responsibilities?
questions.answer: I keep coding, but deliberately: small non-critical stories, tooling, and reviews that teach. I don't own the core of a feature the release depends on, since my time is unpredictable. I hand tracks to seniors, which grows them and frees me.
questions.keyTakeaway: Code for judgment and teaching, not for the critical path; grow seniors to hold tracks.

questions.question: How do you drive adoption of a new standard or technology the team does not want?
questions.answer: I start by understanding the objection, because teams resisting change are usually protecting delivery. Then I back the case with a spike or benchmark and pilot with a volunteer pair. I make the new path easy with templates, set a sunset date with the team, and hold it. If the pilot proves them right, I drop it.
questions.keyTakeaway: Listen, prove with a pilot, make the new path easy, then hold the sunset date.

questions.question: You inherit a struggling team, morale is low and delivery is slipping, so what do your first 90 days look like?
questions.answer: Month one I listen: one-on-ones with every engineer, stakeholders, delivery history and incidents, and I change nothing visible. I name two or three constraints causing pain and play them back to the team. Month two I land one visible quick win that removes real friction, like a flaky pipeline. Month three I agree a few measurable commitments with product.
questions.keyTakeaway: Diagnose before changing anything, spend credibility on one visible win, then commit to few measurable goals.

questions.question: How do you decide what to delegate and what to keep on your own plate?
questions.answer: I keep what's mine: decisions that cross teams, people matters with career consequences, and representing the team upward. For everything else I ask whether it's reversible and whether it would grow someone. If both, I delegate with context and a check-in. The quality bar stays with me.
questions.keyTakeaway: Delegate reversible work that grows people; keep cross-team decisions, career conversations, and the quality bar.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you said no to a senior stakeholder and still kept the relationship strong.
questions.answer: A VP wanted a big client feature mid-quarter, during a committed platform migration. I spent a day building the trade-off: what it displaces, the added risk, and two cheaper alternatives. I presented it as a choice, on one page, in person. They picked the smaller option and it shipped in two weeks.
questions.keyTakeaway: Say no to the request, not the person: bring costs plus alternatives and let them choose.

questions.question: How do you negotiate a technical debt budget with a product manager who wants only features?
questions.answer: I argue delivery cost, not debt. I measure friction: days the last three features lost to workarounds, incidents traced to a shaky module. Then I price debt work like features and ask for a standing share, like one engineer per sprint or twenty percent. With no delivery or incident story, I stop asking.
questions.keyTakeaway: Price debt in delivery cost, request a standing capacity rule, and only ask for items with a proven friction story.

questions.question: What signal do you look for when interviewing senior engineers, beyond coding ability?
questions.answer: The strongest signal is what they do at ambiguity and disagreement, since seniors are hired for judgment, not speed. I probe a real system they owned: what they'd tear down first, what broke after they left, and what they'd change now. I also watch the scope of their care, like operability and maintainers. Red flags are being unable to name a mistake.
questions.keyTakeaway: Hire for judgment under ambiguity, scope of care beyond code, and honest reflection on past systems.

questions.question: How do you get a senior hire productive and trusted within their first month?
questions.answer: Before they start I assign a buddy who isn't me, line up a small real change for week one, and book introductions. The first task is low-risk but end to end, touching the deploy path and runbooks. They get a written architecture map, and at week three I ask for a fresh-eyes memo and act on one point publicly.
questions.keyTakeaway: Real end-to-end work early, a written architecture map, and a fresh-eyes memo the team visibly acts on.

questions.question: How do you run architecture reviews that keep quality up without becoming a gatekeeping bottleneck?
questions.answer: I keep review light: a pre-read under two pages, thirty minutes mostly of questions, and the author as the decision owner, not a committee. Objections need a concrete failure mode or cost. Heavy process is for irreversible choices like data models and public contracts. If a review catches nothing, I shorten it.
questions.keyTakeaway: Reserve scrutiny for irreversible decisions, require concrete objections, and shrink the review when it stops catching real problems.

questions.question: How do you measure engineering health without falling into the velocity-metrics trap?
questions.answer: I ask three questions: can we deliver, can we operate, can we sustain the people. For delivery I use lead time and change-failure rate, not story points, which measure activity. For operability I look at incident frequency and time to recover. Sustainability is mostly qualitative: survey signals on load and clarity, who is single-threaded, and whether the maintenance share drifts up. I review numbers with the team, never as a leaderboard, so a dip starts a conversation about causes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Measure deliverability, operability, and sustainability as outcomes reviewed with the team, never as leaderboards.

questions.question: How do you manage up and influence decisions your own boss makes?
questions.answer: My boss has their own bosses and budget, so I speak in business risk, cost, and customer impact. I never surface a surprise late. If a date slips, I say so early with options, because leaders forgive problems they knew about. To change a decision, I bring a recommendation and trade-offs.
questions.keyTakeaway: No late surprises, risks in business language, recommendations with trade-offs, and a record that keeps your boss informed effortlessly.

questions.question: How do you align technology choices across teams you have no authority over?
questions.answer: Without authority, my currency is evidence and goodwill. I propose agreements only at the seams where teams collide, like API contracts and shared libraries. I shop a short proposal with each lead first, so the meeting ratifies instead of ambushes. Contested choices get a small pilot, and I help with their migration first.
questions.keyTakeaway: Align at the seams with pre-negotiated proposals, evidence from pilots, and goodwill banked before it is spent.

questions.question: How do you handle it when a historically strong engineer's performance drops?
questions.answer: Strong people underperform for reasons: workload, unclear expectations, a stalled project, or something outside work. I talk early and privately, and name the specific gap. We agree two or three concrete changes with check-ins, and I fix what's mine. If nothing improves in a set window, I escalate formally with HR, never as an ambush.
questions.keyTakeaway: Diagnose early and privately, name the gap concretely, agree on changes with a deadline, then escalate without ambush.

questions.question: What are you doing to make yourself replaceable as a technical lead?
questions.answer: Succession is a design problem. I list what only I do and move one item per quarter to a named senior with real ownership. I write decision records so my successor inherits judgment, not just state. I also tell my boss, since a lead seen as irreplaceable gets passed over for promotion.
questions.keyTakeaway: Transfer one irreplaceable duty per quarter to a named senior and write down the judgment so it survives you.

questions.question: As a lead, how do you keep your technical skills sharp while your calendar fills with management work?
questions.answer: I won't out-code my seniors on their stacks, so I aim for current judgment: what's changing, why it matters, and when to bet. I prototype one emerging technology per quarter against a real internal problem, not a tutorial, and read other teams' RFCs and postmortems. I also teach, because explaining exposes gaps.
questions.keyTakeaway: Stay current through real prototypes, others' RFCs and postmortems, and teaching, aiming for current judgment not coding speed.

questions.question: When you cannot enforce every standard at once, how do you choose which battles to fight first?
questions.answer: I rank standards by blast radius and reversibility, not annoyance. Correctness and safety come first, like security and data handling, because failures there are expensive and irreversible. Next come standards with compounding payoff, like observability. Style comes last, since linters settle that mechanically. Each standard needs a paved path, or the team drops it under pressure.
questions.keyTakeaway: Enforce by blast radius and reversibility: safety first, compounding standards next, style to linters not personal capital.

questions.question: How do you lead during a production incident while keeping the post-incident culture blameless?
questions.answer: During an incident my job is roles and rhythm, not fixes. I name an incident commander for the technical response and a comms owner for stakeholders, and set a short update cadence. I optimize for restoration over root cause and never ask who did it. Afterward I build a timeline from artifacts, name contributing factors instead of a culprit, and track owned action items.
questions.keyTakeaway: Separate incident command from communication, optimize for restoration, and prove blamelessness by how the review treats people.

questions.question: How do you present deeply technical trade-offs to an executive audience without losing the substance?
questions.answer: Executives need the shape of the decision, not the design. I frame trade-offs in money, time, and customer risk, like 'A ships in March and slows every later change, B ships in June and each change stays cheap'. I give my recommendation and the condition under which I'd flip it, and I never bluff.
questions.keyTakeaway: Translate trade-offs into money, time, and risk; recommend with a stated flip condition; never bluff past a question.

questions.question: Walk me through how you decide between building a capability and buying or adopting one.
questions.answer: I ask whether the capability differentiates us. I buy commodity and build what carries our identity, so auth and payments get bought. I price the full cost of building, including years of maintenance and on-call, and weigh lock-in on the buy side. I run a time-boxed proof of concept and write the exit plan before signing.
questions.keyTakeaway: Buy commodity, build differentiators, price total maintenance honestly, and write the exit plan before committing.

questions.question: How do you give difficult technical feedback to a peer lead you do not manage?
questions.answer: I do it quickly and in private, because feedback that waits for a formal setting reads as an ambush. I open with a shared goal, then describe observable behavior and its cost, like schema changes shipped without contract review that caused two downstream breakages. I ask for their read first, since peers hold context I lack. I never use feedback as a status move.
questions.keyTakeaway: Peer feedback works when it is private, specific, anchored to a shared goal, and never a status move.
